subject: 2023-count
title: Number of Ways to Traverse a Grid

plan.A: Develop a candidate using sparse obstacle counting: deduplicate blocked coordinates, sort them by x+y, and use binomial path counts modulo 1,000,000,007 to compute paths that avoid earlier blocked cells, then subtract paths through blocked cells from the unobstructed total. Precompute factorials and inverse factorials through 2N−2. Handle blocked start/end, duplicates, dominance, and N=1 correctly. Keep memory O(N+M); do not assume obstacles are sparse enough to make O(M²) fast on every input.
plan.B: Develop a memory-light one-dimensional grid DP with blocked coordinates stored by row, avoiding the baseline's O(N²) blocked-cell allocation. Explore an adaptive candidate that chooses between this O(N²)-time scan and sparse obstacle counting using input-dependent work estimates and measured crossovers. Preserve correctness for all valid inputs; do not tune dispatch based on particular test values.
plan.C: Investigate useful CPU parallelism for the four-core ARM64 target (no GPU). A promising option is batching sparse obstacles with equal x+y: compute each point independently from completed earlier batches, parallelizing only when a batch has enough work. You may also evaluate a tiled or diagonal wavefront for dense DP, but account for synchronization overhead. Retain a serial path for small workloads and verify all dependencies and modular arithmetic.
plan.G: Integrate the strongest measured candidate(s) from A, B, and C, including a serial or adaptive path where appropriate. Re-run correctness and timing on the integrated program rather than assuming gains combine: the baseline is correct on 4 cases and measured 0.0798277 seconds mean across 3 samples (score 0.5), but no case dimensions are reported. Compare complete-program measurements, preserve correctness for every valid input, and do not alter tests, oracle, compiler, budgets, target, permissions, or source beyond the optimization work.
plan.analysis: The supplied source solves the grid-path problem with O(N²) time and O(N²) blocked-grid storage, which is the clearest scaling opportunity given N<200,000 and potentially sparse obstacles. Sparse combinatorial counting can reduce work when M is small, while a one-dimensional DP provides a complementary robust fallback; neither should be presumed fastest for every input. The recorded baseline supplies a correctness result and timing but no workload dimensions, so recommendations should be validated empirically rather than inferred from specific tests.

plan.A: Refine the fastest measured approach (program 97b103d05aca4f1e, 0.02305 s): preserve the one-row DP and sorted obstacle sweep, and focus on reducing fallback per-cell and obstacle-lookup overhead. Benchmark changes against this candidate across workload sizes; keep the DP correct for every valid obstacle configuration.
plan.B: Explore an obstacle-centric algorithm and a defensible crossover to the dense DP fallback. Prior combinatorial candidates measured 0.07372 s and 0.10976 s, while the SIMD hybrid measured 0.05378 s—all slower than the best result—so diagnose their costs rather than carrying them over unchanged. Account for obstacle count, deduplication, endpoint blocks, and modular arithmetic; avoid a quadratic obstacle-pair path when its estimated work exceeds the grid scan.
plan.C: Improve the measured anti-diagonal wavefront approach (0.02591 s), which is competitive but slower than the best candidate. On the four-core ARM64 target, investigate tiled wavefront work to reduce per-diagonal synchronization and scheduling overhead, retaining a low-overhead sequential path for small workloads. Preserve the true DP dependencies and validate all obstacle cases.
plan.G: Use the fastest measured candidate, A's 97b103d05aca4f1e, as the integration baseline. Incorporate B or C ideas only when their isolated measurements justify them, with a workload-based dispatch if needed; do not assume their gains add when combined. Measure and correctness-check the complete integrated program, including small grids, duplicate obstacles, and blocked endpoints, against the same harness.
plan.analysis: This is Problem D: the baseline uses O(N²) blocked-cell storage and O(N²) DP work. The strongest measured candidate replaces dense obstacle storage with a sorted obstacle sweep and one-row DP, reducing mean time from 0.07983 s to 0.02305 s. The wavefront candidate measured 0.02591 s; the in-place DP candidate measured 0.04788 s. Other measured combinatorial/SIMD variants were slower (0.05378–0.10976 s), so further algorithmic branches need evidence and a crossover that reflects their actual costs. Favor measured, correctness-preserving improvements; do not assume integration is additive.
